description: Tonoteam Ultimate is a team of Systems and Computing Engineering students from Universidad Tecnológica de Bolívar, Colombia. We are passionate about data analysis focused on generating tangible solutions, effective data interpretation and visualization, and developing technological applications that turn information into practical tools capable of creating real-world impact and addressing meaningful problems.
summary:
VITRUVIO is an autonomous crew health monitoring prototype for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. A crew member records a daily check-in of vital signs; the engine scores it with the unmodified NEWS2 chart from the Royal College of Physicians, compares readings against a personal baseline and against cited absolute clinical limits, and plans contact escalation across transit, station, rover and base environments — including the communication round-trip delay.

Everything the app shows is traceable: manual records stay on-device, simulated data is labelled as such, and every clinical band, limit and care step cites its source. It is a mission simulation prototype, not medical advice or a flight-certified clinical system.
details:
VITRUVIO is an offline-capable health monitoring prototype designed for a difficult question: how can astronauts understand changes in their health when medical expertise is far away and communication with Earth is delayed?

The application brings measurements, personal trends, measurement instructions, and emergency guidance into one visual workspace. Its central interface is an interactive 3D anatomical body. Users select a body system to explore its indicators, understand their relevance, and access related guidance. Male and female anatomical models are available, alongside an interactive 2D alternative. Multiple crew members can maintain separate local profiles, each with their own measurements, history, and personal baseline.

Crew members manually enter health observations such as blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, oxygen saturation, sleep, and mood. VITRUVIO combines the NEWS2 early warning score with personal baselines and separately cited reference rules to make changes easier to interpret. Missing observations remain visible: the application does not invent values or present an incomplete assessment as a reassuring result. Historical views help users distinguish an isolated reading from a developing pattern.

The workflow extends beyond recording numbers. Measurement guides explain which instrument to use and how to take a reading. Emergency scenarios provide branching instructions, timers, and a record of confirmed actions. Mission scenarios—including an orbital station, transit spacecraft, rover, and planetary base—provide context for communication delays and escalation planning. An exportable report brings together measurements, assessment completeness, mission context, and recorded actions to support a structured handover.

NASA’s open data and technical resources made several specific parts of this workflow possible:

  • NASA Human Research Program: A selected set of 11 risks across five spaceflight hazards connects health monitoring to mission conditions. These resources inform how risks relate to body systems, environmental context, and measurement guidance.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository, OSD-575: Inspiration4 blood chemistry observations provide real astronaut reference bands for glucose, calcium, sodium, and potassium in the trends interface. The application identifies these as observations from a small cohort—four crew members and 28 samples—rather than clinical limits or the user’s personal baseline.
  • NASA-STD-3001 and Canadian Space Agency resources: The radiation module uses NASA’s standard as a reference for recorded exposure, including its 600 mSv career limit, while CSA material provides explanatory context. The interface distinguishes personal exposure limits from spacecraft design requirements.
  • NASA’s 2015 ISS medical kit checklist: Measurement guides identify instruments and, where documented, their pack and slot. Missing information is acknowledged, and the checklist is clearly identified as historical rather than today’s onboard inventory.

Creatively, VITRUVIO turns the body into an interface and connects scientific references to the places where users need them. A source is more useful when it helps explain a trend, identify an instrument, or understand a mission hazard. The visual design follows the language of mission instrumentation: clear hierarchy, restrained use of color, contextual labels, and focused inspection of body systems.

We developed the application with TypeScript, React, and Vite; Three.js and React Three Fiber support the anatomical visualization and mission environments. Zustand manages application state, while Dexie and IndexedDB store records locally. Service workers support offline operation after the initial online setup, with installation available through compatible browsers. Vitest and Playwright support automated verification. The prototype runs on ordinary computers, tablets, and phones; measurements are entered manually, without requiring connected medical hardware.

Our team considered limited connectivity, privacy, workload, accessibility, missing data, and the need to explain where information comes from. The application includes reduced-motion support, a 2D body alternative, and status information that does not rely on color alone. Demonstration data remains separate from manually recorded observations.

The intended impact is to support crew autonomy, reduce the effort of organizing health information, and make changes easier to communicate. The same approach could eventually benefit remote clinics and field teams on Earth. VITRUVIO remains a competition prototype: it does not diagnose, prescribe, or replace professional care, and operational medical use would require further validation.
